kurals.tamil:
உற்றநோய் நோன்றல் உயிர்க்குறுகண் செய்யாமை
அற்றே தவத்திற் குரு.
kurals.transliteration:
Utra noi nondral uyirkku urukan seyyaamai
Atre thavaththirku uru.
kurals.meaning: To bear patiently whatever suffering comes to oneself, and never to inflict suffering on any other living being: this, and nothing more, is the true form of penance.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone bumps into you and it hurts. Penance, says Valluvar, is two simple things: you put up with the hurt without making a fuss, and you never hurt anyone back or hurt anyone at all. That is what being a real ‘tapas’ person looks like.
kurals.university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a definition that is striking for what it leaves out: no fire rituals, no fasting regimens, no forest hermitage, only a two-part ethical formula — endurance (நோன்றல், noṉṟal) of suffering that befalls oneself, and non-infliction (செய்யாமை) of suffering on other lives. The emphatic அற்றே (‘just that much’) deliberately reduces tapas from spectacle to disposition. Parimelazhagar notes that the suffering endured includes both what arises naturally (hunger, cold, illness) and what others inflict, which aligns the verse closely with the Jain and Buddhist redefinition of austerity as patience plus ahiṃsā. The move is thus both conservative (it keeps the prestigious word ‘tapas’) and reformist (it ethicizes it), and it frames every later claim in the chapter about the ‘power’ of tapas as resting on this moral foundation.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of the body consists in worship of the Supreme Lord, the brāhmaṇas, the spiritual master, and superiors like the father and mother, and in cleanliness, simplicity, celibacy and nonviolence.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita breaks tapas into bodily, verbal and mental kinds, and places nonviolence (ahiṃsā) inside the very definition of bodily austerity.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Gita makes not-harming part of what tapas is; Valluvar goes further by making it half the whole definition and pairing it with endurance.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the ahiṃsā component; Gita’s list is broader and ritual-inclusive, lacking the endurance half.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what glory is it, if, when ye be buffeted for your faults, ye shall take it patiently? but if, when ye do well, and suffer for it, ye take it patiently, this is acceptable with God.”
christianity.explanation: Peter tells believers that patiently enduring undeserved suffering, without striking back, is what pleases God.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts define spiritual worth as bearing pain patiently while refusing to retaliate.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on endurance and implicit non-retaliation; not framed as a definition of asceticism.

islam.quote_or_event: “Fasting is a shield (or a screen or a shelter). So, the person observing fasting should avoid sexual relation with his wife and should not behave foolishly and impudently, and if somebody fights with him or abuses him, he should tell him twice, ‘I am fasting.’”
islam.explanation: The Prophet describes sawm not merely as going hungry but as a discipline in which the faster absorbs provocation without answering it with harm.
islam.tie_back: The Islamic fast, like Valluvar’s tapas, joins bodily endurance with a refusal to hurt others even when provoked.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close structural match: ascetic endurance plus non-retaliation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “About those who are insulted and do not insult, who hear their shame and do not respond, who act out of love and are joyful in suffering, the verse says: ‘And they that love Him are as the sun going forth in its might’.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud praises those who absorb insult without returning it and who accept suffering with joy, likening them to the rising sun.
judaism.tie_back: Endure what comes, harm no one in return — the same two pillars Valluvar names as the whole of tapas.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on both components; not labelled as ‘penance’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Enduring patience is the highest austerity. ‘Nibbana is supreme,’ say the Buddhas. He is not a true monk who harms another, nor a true renunciate who oppresses others.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha redefines tapas as patient endurance and declares that anyone who harms others is not a genuine renunciant.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost a restatement of the Kural: austerity = patience + not harming others.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near-verbatim conceptual match, including the word ‘austerity’ (tapo).

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus, disguised as a beggar in his own house, bears the suitors’ insults and blows night after night, commanding his own heart to endure rather than lash out.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s hero is celebrated for polytlas — much-enduring — self-command under humiliation.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Mirrors the endurance half of Valluvar’s definition; the non-harm half fails, since Odysseus later slaughters the suitors.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Endurance matches; the restraint is tactical, not ahiṃsā.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “These two words, he said, are ἀνέχου (bear) and ἀπέχου (forbear).”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus taught that the two worst faults are failing to endure what must be endured and failing to refrain from what must be avoided; ‘bear and forbear’ would make a person almost sinless.
philosophy.tie_back: The Stoic two-word rule is a near twin of Valluvar’s two-part definition of tapas.
philosophy.source: Epictetus in Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights 17.19.5-6 (trans. J. C. Rolfe)
philosophy._accuracy_note: ‘Forbear’ covers self-restraint broadly rather than non-harm specifically, but the two-part structure is striking.

kurals.tamil:
தவமும் தவமுடையார்க்கு ஆகும் அதனை
அஃதிலார் மேற்கொள் வது.
kurals.transliteration:
Thavamum thavamudaiyaarkku aagum adhanai
Aqdhilaar merkolvadhu.
kurals.meaning: Penance bears fruit only for those who truly possess the inner quality of penance; for those who lack it, taking up its outward form is a futile effort.
kurals.elementary: Wearing a doctor’s coat does not make you a doctor. In the same way, putting on the clothes and habits of a holy person does not work unless you really have the patience and goodness inside.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on a pun-like repetition: தவம் (tapas) comes only to those who have தவம். Commentators split on what the second ‘tapas’ means. Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah read it karmically — only those who accumulated tapas in earlier births can undertake it now — while Mu. Varadarasan reads it as a warning against தவக்கோலம், the ascetic costume adopted without ascetic conduct. The second reading anticipates the very next chapter, கூடாவொழுக்கம் (‘Imposture’), and fits Valluvar’s habitual suspicion of form without substance. Either way, the verse asserts that tapas is not a technique anyone can pick up but the outward expression of an already-formed inner capacity.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those who undergo severe austerities and penances not recommended in the scriptures, performing them out of pride and egoism, who are impelled by lust and attachment, who are foolish and who torture the material elements of the body as well as the Supersoul dwelling within, are to be known as demons.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna condemns austerity performed by those whose inner disposition is proud and desirous — the outward act is present but the right nature is not.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts insist that tapas without the proper inner quality is worthless or worse.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Gita is harsher (calls it demonic); Kural simply calls it futile.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns against fasting as a public performance; the show earns only human notice, not God’s reward.
christianity.tie_back: Matches Varadarasan’s reading: the ascetic ‘look’ without the ascetic reality is empty.
christianity._accuracy_note: Targets hypocrisy specifically; Kural also allows a karmic-capacity reading.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever does not give up forged speech and evil actions, Allah is not in need of his leaving his food and drink.”
islam.explanation: A fast that leaves the character unchanged is declared meaningless in God’s sight.
islam.tie_back: The outward discipline without the inner reality is futile — Valluvar’s exact verdict.
islam._accuracy_note: Close match on futility of external austerity divorced from conduct.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Is it such a fast that I have chosen? a day for a man to afflict his soul? is it to bow down his head as a bulrush, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? wilt thou call this a fast, and an acceptable day to the LORD?”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah mocks ritual fasting and sackcloth performed by people whose conduct stays unjust, and redefines the true fast as freeing the oppressed.
judaism.tie_back: Both reject the costume of penance when the substance is missing.
judaism._accuracy_note: Prophetic social-justice emphasis; same core logic.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What is the use of your matted hair, O witless man? What of your garment of antelope’s hide? Within you is the tangle (of passion); only outwardly do you cleanse yourself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha ridicules the ascetic whose matted locks and deerskin conceal an untamed mind.
buddhism.tie_back: Precisely the ‘tavakkōlam’ critique: the ascetic garb is useless without the inner tapas.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close; even the imagery (ascetic dress) matches commentarial readings.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Phaethon begs his father Helios to let him drive the sun-chariot; lacking the strength and skill for it, he loses control, scorches the earth, and is struck down by Zeus.
greek_mythology.explanation: A task suited only to one with the proper power ends in ruin when attempted by one without it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Illustrates the Kural’s principle that a discipline belongs only to those with the capacity for it; others who take it up fail.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Structural analogy only; not about asceticism.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus warns that whoever takes up the Cynic’s cloak, wallet and staff without the inner preparation and divine calling undertakes a great matter in vain and makes himself ridiculous.
philosophy.explanation: For Epictetus the Cynic life is a vocation for the rare person fitted for it, not a costume anyone may wear.
philosophy.tie_back: A close philosophical parallel: the ascetic life ‘belongs to’ those who possess its inner qualification.
philosophy.source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.22 (On the Calling of a Cynic)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong match to the ‘qualified practitioner’ reading.

kurals.tamil:
துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி மறந்தார்கொல்
மற்றை யவர்கள் தவம்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thurandhaarkku thuppuravu vendi marandhaarkol
Matraiyavargal thavam.
kurals.meaning: Is it perhaps because they wished to provide food and necessities for the renunciants that everyone else has forgotten to do penance themselves?
kurals.elementary: Picture a whole village cooking lunch for a few hermits on the hill. Valluvar jokes: maybe everyone got so busy packing lunches for the hermits that they forgot to become good and disciplined themselves!
kurals.university: This is one of Valluvar’s rare ironic rhetorical questions (கொல் marks doubt). Read straightforwardly, it offers an indulgent explanation for why so few undertake tapas: society needs householders to feed the ascetics. Read more sharply — as Kalaignar does — it is a rebuke: supporting renunciants is no substitute for one’s own discipline. The verse also documents a real economic structure of early Indian religion, in which Jain, Buddhist and Brahmanical renouncers depended on lay donation, and in which donors believed they shared the merit of those they supported. Valluvar gently punctures the complacency that such a division of spiritual labour could produce.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Manu declares that just as all creatures live by depending on air, so the members of all the other orders of life (students, forest-dwellers, renunciants) subsist by the support of the householder, who is therefore the most excellent order.
hinduism.explanation: Brahmanical law explicitly makes the householder the economic base on which ascetics rely.
hinduism.tie_back: Describes the very arrangement Valluvar is teasing — householders feeding renunciants.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; Manu praises the arrangement while Valluvar ironizes its side-effect.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that receiveth a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward; and he that receiveth a righteous man in the name of a righteous man shall receive a righteous man’s reward.”
christianity.explanation: Those who host and support God’s messengers share in their reward.
christianity.tie_back: Supports the ‘merit through support’ logic that Valluvar suggests has made householders forget their own tapas.
christianity._accuracy_note: Affirms the support-merit link; lacks the Kural’s irony.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Charity is] for the poor who have been restricted for the cause of Allah, unable to move about in the land. An ignorant [person] would think them self-sufficient because of their restraint, but you will know them by their [characteristic] sign.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an directs charity to those wholly devoted to God’s cause who cannot earn for themselves.
islam.tie_back: Parallels lay support of renunciants as a religious duty.
islam._accuracy_note: Same social arrangement; no ironic critique.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rashi explains that the tribe of Zebulun engaged in sea-trade and provided for Issachar, who devoted himself to Torah study, and so Moses blessed Zebulun first — the supporter shares in the scholar’s merit.
judaism.explanation: The ‘Issachar–Zebulun’ partnership became the classic Jewish model of lay support for full-time religious devotion.
judaism.tie_back: A direct counterpart to householders feeding ascetics; Valluvar’s question probes whether the Zebulun role lets one neglect one’s own discipline.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong structural match; lacks the Kural’s ironic edge.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Sangha is praised as the ‘incomparable field of merit for the world’; monks on the dhutanga and alms-round path depend entirely on lay donors, who earn merit by giving.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism formalized the monk–lay relationship: renunciants practise, householders feed them and gain merit.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the arrangement behind Valluvar’s question about why ‘others’ forgot tapas.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; describes the system rather than critiquing it.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The poor old couple Baucis and Philemon feed two disguised gods from their meagre store and are rewarded by being made priests of a temple.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hospitality to the sacred visitor is rewarded with sacred status.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Weak parallel: support of the holy earns merit, but there is no ascetic class or critique.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Only the ‘feeding the holy’ motif overlaps.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s ideal city the guardians own no property and receive their sustenance from the producing citizens as a wage for their guardianship.
philosophy.explanation: Plato builds a division of labour in which a disciplined, propertyless elite is maintained by others.
philosophy.tie_back: Resembles the lay–ascetic economy Valluvar describes, though Plato’s guardians are rulers, not penitents.

kurals.tamil:
ஒன்னார்த் தெறலும் உவந்தாரை ஆக்கலும்
எண்ணின் தவத்தான் வரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Onnaar theralum uvandhaarai aakkalum
Ennin thavaththaan varum.
kurals.meaning: If the ascetic so wills it, both the destruction of enemies and the raising up of those who love him can be accomplished through the power of penance alone.
kurals.elementary: In old stories, people who did very long and sincere penance got special powers — like a superhero who trained for years. Valluvar says such a person could, just by wishing it, stop bad people and help good friends.
kurals.university: Here Valluvar adopts the widespread Indian belief that tapas generates real, even cosmic, power — the power to curse (சாபம்) and to bless (அருள்), as Parimelazhagar glosses ஆற்றல் in the neighbouring verse. The conditional எண்ணின் (‘if he wills’) is crucial: after 261 defined the ascetic as one who harms no one, the implication is that such power exists but is normally left unused. The verse thus holds a tension typical of Indian ascetic literature, where rishis like Vishvamitra or Durvasa possess destructive capacity that their own ethic ought to restrain. Modern commentators such as Kalaignar demythologize it as the practical power of resolve and self-control.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Vishvamitra, having amassed great tapas, uses its power to raise his devotee King Trishanku bodily toward heaven and, when the gods cast him down, creates a new constellation of heavens for him.
hinduism.explanation: The Ramayana’s famous episode shows tapas as a force that can uplift a friend in defiance even of the gods.
hinduism.tie_back: A textbook illustration of ‘uplifting those who love him’ through tapas; Vishvamitra elsewhere also curses his foes.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-exact narrative embodiment of the Kural.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And Elijah answered and said to the captain of fifty, If I be a man of God, then let fire come down from heaven, and consume thee and thy fifty. And there came down fire from heaven, and consumed him and his fifty.”
christianity.explanation: The ascetic prophet Elijah calls down fire on the soldiers sent to seize him.
christianity.tie_back: A holy man’s spiritual standing directly destroys his enemies, as the Kural says tapas can.
christianity._accuracy_note: Power flows from God’s favour rather than accumulated austerity; Jesus later rebukes such use (Luke 9:54-55).

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah said, ‘I will declare war against him who shows hostility to a pious worshipper of Mine… and if he asks Me, I will give him, and if he asks My protection (Refuge), I will protect him.’”
islam.explanation: One who draws near through extra devotions gains God’s protection against enemies and has requests granted.
islam.tie_back: Devotional discipline yields both defeat of foes and fulfilment of wishes, though the agent is God, not the ascetic’s own power.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match; theocentric rather than self-generated power.

judaism.quote_or_event: After twelve years hiding in a cave in study and deprivation, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and his son emerged with such spiritual intensity that whatever they gazed upon was burned, until a heavenly voice sent them back.
judaism.explanation: The Talmud portrays ascetic withdrawal as generating a dangerous, destructive spiritual force.
judaism.tie_back: Close to the Kural’s claim that tapas can destroy; the story also criticizes its unrestrained use.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong parallel including the ethical tension.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha lists supernormal powers (iddhi) — multiplying the body, passing through walls, walking on water — as fruits of the concentrated mind of the disciplined monk, while elsewhere forbidding their display.
buddhism.explanation: Early Buddhism accepts that meditative discipline yields extraordinary powers but treats them as secondary and potentially dangerous.
buddhism.tie_back: Agrees that discipline yields power; differs in never endorsing its use to destroy enemies.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Power-from-discipline matches; destructive application is rejected.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Chryses, priest of Apollo, is insulted by Agamemnon; he prays to Apollo, who sends a plague of arrows upon the Greek army.
greek_mythology.explanation: A holy man’s standing with a god becomes a weapon against those who wrong him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Resembles the ‘destruction of enemies’ power of the Kural’s ascetic, but grounded in priestly service, not austerity.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Priestly, not ascetic; power is the god’s.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plotinus argues that the sage who has turned inward to contemplation cannot be touched by magic spells and that only the irrational part of a person is subject to such forces.
philosophy.explanation: Neoplatonism grants the contemplative a kind of invulnerability but not active power over others.
philosophy.tie_back: A distant parallel: the disciplined soul gains power, but only defensive, never used to harm or promote others.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Weak; philosophy generally rejects curse-and-blessing powers.

kurals.tamil:
வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங் கெய்தலால் செய்தவம்
ஈண்டு முயலப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vendiya vendiyaangu eydhalaal seydhavam
Eendu muyalap padum.
kurals.meaning: Because through it one obtains whatever one desires, exactly as one desires it, penance should be earnestly pursued here and now, in this very life.
kurals.elementary: If you practise the piano every day, one day you can play any song you want, just the way you want. Valluvar says tapas is like that for your whole life — so start practising now, not later.
kurals.university: The verse gives the motivational logic of tapas: it is effective, delivering desired ends ‘as desired’ (வேண்டியாங்கு). ஈண்டு (‘here’) is read by Parimelazhagar as ‘in this birth’, urging urgency, while Mu. Varadarasan reads it as ‘even in the householder’s state’, democratizing tapas beyond the forest. The claim sits in tension with the Gita’s ideal of desireless action and with Valluvar’s own later chapter on the destruction of desire (அவா அறுத்தல்); commentators resolve this by noting that for the truly austere the highest ‘desire’ is liberation itself. The couplet thus captures tapas at its most instrumental while quietly pointing beyond instrumentality.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The child Dhruva, rejected by his father, performs severe tapas in the forest of Madhuvana; Vishnu appears and grants him a kingdom and ultimately the eternal pole-star position.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata Purana’s Dhruva story is the paradigm of tapas yielding exactly what the practitioner sought, and more.
hinduism.tie_back: Embodies ‘obtaining what one desires, as one desires’ through tapas.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match; Dhruva famously renounces his original wish when he sees Vishnu.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But thou, when thou fastest, anoint thine head, and wash thy face; That thou appear not unto men to fast, but unto thy Father which is in secret: and thy Father, which seeth in secret, shall reward thee openly.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus assures that sincere, hidden fasting will be rewarded by God.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts affirm that real austerity produces real results; Jesus stresses secrecy.
christianity._accuracy_note: Reward promised, though not ‘whatever one desires’.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah said, ‘All the deeds of Adam’s sons (people) are for them, except fasting which is for Me, and I will give the reward for it.’”
islam.explanation: Fasting is singled out as the act whose reward God personally bestows, beyond ordinary measure.
islam.tie_back: Affirms the unique efficacy of ascetic discipline that motivates the Kural’s call to pursue it.
islam._accuracy_note: Reward emphasis matches; not phrased as wish-fulfilment.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Then said he unto me, Fear not, Daniel: for from the first day that thou didst set thine heart to understand, and to chasten thyself before thy God, thy words were heard, and I am come for thy words.”
judaism.explanation: After three weeks of fasting and mourning, Daniel is told his self-affliction secured an answer from heaven.
judaism.tie_back: Self-chastening directly obtains what was sought — the logic of this Kural.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close; the ‘desire’ is understanding, not general wishes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In his first sermon the Buddha rejects both indulgence in sense pleasures and devotion to self-mortification as extremes, teaching the Middle Way after his own years of extreme austerity failed to bring awakening.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism explicitly denies that harsh bodily austerity reliably delivers the highest goal.
buddhism.tie_back: An instructive contrast: Buddhism shares the goal-orientation but disputes that severe tapas is the means.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But between us and Goodness the gods have placed the sweat of our brows; long and steep is the path that leads to her, and it is rough at the first.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod teaches that excellence and prosperity are gained only through hard toil, which becomes easy once the summit is reached.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s conviction that strenuous discipline is the reliable road to what one seeks.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 289-291 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Toil rather than penance; aim is excellence and livelihood.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For of all things good and fair, the gods give nothing to man without toil and effort.”
philosophy.explanation: In Prodicus’ fable of Heracles at the crossroads, Virtue tells the young hero that every good thing is earned by labour.
philosophy.tie_back: Same principle as the Kural: disciplined effort is the price and the guarantee of every desired good.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on effort-yields-goods; secular ethic of toil.

kurals.tamil:
தவஞ்செய்வார் தங்கருமஞ் செய்வார்மற் றல்லார்
அவஞ்செய்வார் ஆசையுட் பட்டு.
kurals.transliteration:
Thavanjeyvaar thangarumanj seyvaar matru allaar
Avanjeyvaar aasaiyut pattu.
kurals.meaning: Those who practise penance are the ones truly doing their own proper work; all others, caught in the net of desire, only labour for their own ruin.
kurals.elementary: Think of a fly stuck in a spider’s web — the more it wriggles, the more stuck it gets. Valluvar says people who chase every want are like that fly, while people who practise self-control are doing the one job that really helps them.
kurals.university: The couplet rests on a sonic antithesis — தவம் (tavam, penance) against அவம் (avam, futility or self-harm) — so that tapas and its absence differ by a single consonant. தம் கருமம் (‘their own work’) implies that spiritual self-cultivation is a person’s genuine duty, while the ‘busy’ worldly life is in fact a failure to act for oneself. Parimelazhagar glosses அவம் as bringing harm upon oneself, since desire-driven action produces karmic bondage. The verse inverts ordinary valuations: the ascetic who seems idle is the only one truly working, and the striving householder, if driven by desire, is idle in the deepest sense.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is lust only, Arjuna, which is born of contact with the material mode of passion and later transformed into wrath, and which is the all-devouring sinful enemy of this world.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names desire (kāma) as the root enemy that devours those it entangles.
hinduism.tie_back: Same diagnosis: desire (ஆசை) turns human effort into self-destruction.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close on desire-as-enemy; lacks the Kural’s contrast with tapas as ‘one’s own work’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that worldly gain pursued at the soul’s expense is ultimate loss.
christianity.tie_back: Mirrors தவம்/அவம்: desire-driven success is really self-ruin.

islam.quote_or_event: “But as for he who feared the position of his Lord and prevented the soul from [unlawful] inclination, Then indeed, Paradise will be [his] refuge.”
islam.explanation: Restraining the self from its desires (the basis of Sufi riyāḍa, self-discipline) is the path to salvation.
islam.tie_back: The self-restrained do their true work; the desire-led lose — the Kural’s dichotomy.
islam._accuracy_note: Close; the Qur’an adds fear of God as motive.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Elazar Ha-kappar said: envy, lust and [the desire for] honor put a man out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah teaches that appetites and ambitions drive a person to ruin.
judaism.tie_back: Same verdict as the Kural on those ‘caught in desire’.
judaism._accuracy_note: Matches the negative half; no explicit ascetic counterpart.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Those who are lust-infatuated fall back into the swirling current (of samsara) like a spider on its self-spun web. This, too, the wise cut off. Without any longing, they abandon all suffering and renounce the world.”
buddhism.explanation: Desire is a self-spun trap; the wise cut it and renounce.
buddhism.tie_back: The same two paths: renunciation as true work, desire as self-made entanglement (ஆசையுட் பட்டு).
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close, including the net/web imagery.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Erysichthon, cursed with insatiable hunger for cutting down Demeter’s sacred grove, devours all his wealth, sells his own daughter, and finally eats his own body.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s grim tale shows appetite consuming its owner.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A vivid image of desire-driven activity that is ultimately self-destruction (அவம்).
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on the negative half; no ascetic foil.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates asks his fellow Athenians whether they are not ashamed to care so much about wealth, reputation and honour while giving no thought to wisdom, truth and the improvement of their souls.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates redefines a person’s real business as care of the soul.
philosophy.tie_back: Matches தம் கருமம் — the self-cultivator alone does his proper work; the acquisitive neglect it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; philosophical rather than ascetic self-cultivation.

kurals.tamil:
சுடச்சுடரும் பொன்போல் ஒளிவிடும் துன்பஞ்
சுடச்சுட நோற்கிற் பவர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Sudachchudarum ponpol olividum thunbanj
Sudachchuda notkirpavarkku.
kurals.meaning: Just as gold shines ever more brightly the more it is heated in the fire, so those who practise penance shine ever more brightly the more suffering burns them.
kurals.elementary: When gold is put in a very hot fire, the dirt burns away and it becomes shinier. Valluvar says hard times do the same for a patient, disciplined person: every difficulty makes them shine brighter.
kurals.university: Among the most celebrated images in the Kural, the verse exploits the reduplicated சுடச்சுட (‘as it burns and burns’) twice — once for the goldsmith’s crucible and once for suffering — binding metaphor and meaning through sound. The figure also restores the etymological heart of tapas, from the Sanskrit root tap, ‘to heat, burn’, a notion also present in the Tamil நோன்பு/நோற்றல் of endurance. Commentators differ on what ‘shines’: Varadarasan and Pappaiah say true knowledge (மெய்யுணர்வு, ஞானம்), Kalaignar says reputation. The refining-fire metaphor is one of the most widely shared images in world religious literature, making this verse unusually rich in parallels.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Rig Veda’s creation hymns describe Order (ṛta) and Truth (satya), and even the first stirring of being, as born from kindled tapas — heat — making ascetic ‘heat’ a cosmogonic force.
hinduism.explanation: In Vedic thought tapas is literally a creative, purifying heat.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar’s gold-in-fire image recovers this primal sense of tapas as burning that produces brilliance.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; conceptual/etymological rather than a direct refining image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ.”
christianity.explanation: Peter likens believers’ trials to the fire that tests gold, producing glory.
christianity.tie_back: Almost the same image: suffering as fire, the sufferer as gold that shines.

islam.quote_or_event: “No fatigue, nor disease, nor sorrow, nor sadness, nor hurt, nor distress befalls a Muslim, even if it were the prick he receives from a thorn, but that Allah expiates some of his sins for that.”
islam.explanation: Every suffering, however small, purifies the believer of sin.
islam.tie_back: Suffering as purification — the refining function of the Kural’s fire.
islam._accuracy_note: Purification theme matches; no gold/radiance image.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And he was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights; he did neither eat bread, nor drink water… Moses wist not that the skin of his face shone while he talked with him.”
judaism.explanation: After forty days of total fasting on Sinai, Moses descends with a face literally radiant.
judaism.tie_back: Austerity endured leads to shining — a striking literal counterpart to ‘shines like gold’.
judaism._accuracy_note: Radiance results from divine encounter, with the fast as its setting.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One by one, little by little, moment by moment, a wise man should remove his own impurities, as a smith removes his dross from silver.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses the metalworker’s refining as the model of gradual self-purification.
buddhism.tie_back: Same smithing metaphor for spiritual refinement.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Metaphor matches; Buddhism emphasises gradual effort rather than suffering.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Demeter, nursing the infant Demophon, secretly places him in the fire each night to burn away his mortality and make him immortal, until his frightened mother interrupts her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Fire here refines a mortal into something divine and deathless.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A mythic counterpart to fire as the agent of transformation into radiance.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Fire-as-purifier matches; the subject is passive, not a penitent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Ignis aurum probat, miseria fortes viros.” (Fire tests gold, misfortune brave men.)
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that God trains good people through hardship, as fire proves gold.
philosophy.tie_back: Nearly identical image and moral: adversity reveals and refines the worthy.

kurals.tamil:
தன்னுயிர் தான்அறப் பெற்றானை ஏனைய
மன்னுயி ரெல்லாந் தொழும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thannuyir thaan arap petraanai enaiya
Mannuyir ellaam thozhum.
kurals.meaning: The one who has completely freed himself from the sense of ‘I’ and ‘my life’ is worshipped by all other living beings in the world.
kurals.elementary: Most of us think ‘me first’. A person who, after lots of practice, stops thinking ‘me, me, me’ becomes so good and gentle that everyone — people and even animals — looks up to them.
kurals.university: The first line is famously compressed: தன்னுயிர் தான் அறப் பெற்றான் can be read as ‘one who has become rid of [attachment to] his own life and of the ego “I”’ (Parimelazhagar, Varadarasan) or as ‘one who has fully gained possession of his own self’ (Pope’s ‘utter self-control’). Both readings converge on self-mastery culminating in egolessness. The consequence — ‘all other enduring lives worship him’ — echoes the Indian belief, also found in Jain and yogic texts, that the ahiṃsā-perfected sage commands the reverence even of animals. Placed after 267, the verse presents egolessness as the gold that emerges from the refining fire.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Patañjali teaches that when a yogi is firmly established in non-violence, hostility is abandoned by all beings in his presence.
hinduism.explanation: The perfected ascetic radiates a peace that transforms how all creatures relate to him.
hinduism.tie_back: Close to ‘all living beings worship him’ — the universal response to the perfected self.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; reverence vs. cessation of hostility.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name: That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow.”
christianity.explanation: Christ’s total self-emptying (kenosis) is followed by universal homage.
christianity.tie_back: Same arc: complete surrender of self leads to worship by all beings.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong structural match; theological subject is unique.

islam.quote_or_event: “Charity does not decrease wealth, no one forgives another except that Allah increases his honor, and no one humbles himself for the sake of Allah except that Allah raises his status.”
islam.explanation: Self-effacement before God leads to exaltation.
islam.tie_back: Egolessness brings honour, as in the Kural.
islam._accuracy_note: Humility → honour matches; ‘worship by all beings’ is stronger in the Kural.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.”
judaism.explanation: Self-mastery is ranked above military conquest.
judaism.tie_back: Affirms the supreme worth of the self-conquered person that the Kural celebrates.
judaism._accuracy_note: Praises self-rule; lacks the universal-reverence consequence.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Even the gods hold dear the wise one, whose senses are subdued like horses well trained by a charioteer, whose pride is destroyed and who is free from the cankers.”
buddhism.explanation: The arahant whose pride is gone is cherished even by the gods.
buddhism.tie_back: Near-exact match: pride (ego) destroyed → revered by all beings, even divine ones.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close in both cause and effect.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Heracles, after completing his grievous labours, is received among the immortals on Olympus, given Hebe as wife, and honoured as a god.
greek_mythology.explanation: Endured toil ends in apotheosis and worship.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Endurance leading to universal honour; but Heracles’ path is heroic, not ego-renouncing.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Outcome matches; the inner egolessness does not.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But verily, if I were not Alexander, I would be Diogenes.”
philosophy.explanation: After the self-denying Cynic asks the world-conqueror merely to stand out of his sun, Alexander confesses his admiration.
philosophy.tie_back: The man who wants nothing commands the reverence even of the most powerful — the Kural’s point in miniature.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 14 (trans. B. Perrin)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Admiration, not worship; Diogenes’ self-denial is proud rather than egoless.

kurals.tamil:
கூற்றம் குதித்தலும் கைகூடும் நோற்றலின்
ஆற்றல் தலைப்பட் டவர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kootram kudhiththalum kaikoodum notralin
Aatral thalaippattavarkku.
kurals.meaning: For those who have attained the power that comes from penance, even leaping beyond Death itself becomes possible.
kurals.elementary: Everyone is scared of death, like a giant monster nobody can beat. Valluvar says a person who has become really strong through tapas can even jump right over that monster.
kurals.university: கூற்றம் (Kūṟṟam), ‘the one who separates [soul from body]’, is the Tamil personification of Death, identified with Yama; குதித்தல் means to leap over or escape. The inclusive உம் (‘even’) signals this as the ultimate limit case of tapas-power, following the curse-and-blessing powers of 264. The medieval commentator Manakkudavar explicitly glosses the verse with the legend of Markandeya, the boy-devotee who escaped Yama’s noose, while Parimelazhagar identifies ஆற்றல் as the power of curse and grace. Philosophically, the verse can also be read as conquest of the fear of death, or as liberation from the cycle of births — interpretations that let the verse speak beyond its mythological frame.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Markandeya, destined to die at sixteen, clings to the Shiva linga in devotion and austerity; when Yama casts his noose, Shiva emerges, kicks Yama away, and grants the boy eternal youth.
hinduism.explanation: Manakkudavar’s own commentary on this Kural cites Markandeya’s escape from death.
hinduism.tie_back: The traditional illustration of ‘leaping beyond Kūṟṟam’ through tapas.
hinduism.source: Markandeya legend (Shaiva Puranas; Tirukkadavur tradition), cited by Manakkudavar on Kural 269
hinduism._accuracy_note: Commentarial tradition itself makes this link.

christianity.quote_or_event: “O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?”
christianity.explanation: Paul proclaims death conquered for the faithful through resurrection.
christianity.tie_back: Shares the claim that death can be overcome; in Christianity through grace rather than accumulated austerity.
christianity._accuracy_note: Victory over death matches; mechanism differs.

islam.quote_or_event: “And never think of those who have been killed in the cause of Allah as dead. Rather, they are alive with their Lord, receiving provision.”
islam.explanation: Those who give themselves wholly for God are not truly subject to death.
islam.tie_back: Supreme self-sacrifice transcends death, a partial echo of the Kural.
islam._accuracy_note: Martyrdom rather than ascetic power; honest next-best.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud relates that the Angel of Death could not take King David because his mouth never ceased from Torah study; only by distracting him for a moment could it approach.
judaism.explanation: Unbroken spiritual discipline held death itself at bay.
judaism.tie_back: Close to the Kural’s image of disciplined power holding off Death.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; discipline is study rather than austerity.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless. Heedlessness is the path to death. The heedful die not. The heedless are as if dead already.”
buddhism.explanation: Sustained vigilance leads to the Deathless (amata), Nibbana.
buddhism.tie_back: Discipline conquers death — understood as release from the round of rebirth.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong; ‘deathless’ is soteriological rather than mythological.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Heracles wrestles Thanatos (Death) at the tomb of Alcestis and forces him to give her back to life.
greek_mythology.explanation: The much-enduring hero physically overpowers Death.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A mythic ‘leap over Death’ by one whose strength was forged through labours.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Other people are likely not to be aware that those who pursue philosophy aright study nothing but dying and being dead.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates says the philosopher’s discipline of detaching soul from body is a rehearsal for death, leaving him unafraid of it.
philosophy.tie_back: The disciplined life overcomes death by mastering it in advance.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Conquest of fear of death rather than escape from it.

kurals.tamil:
இலர்பல ராகிய காரணம் நோற்பார்
சிலர்பலர் நோலா தவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ilar palar aagiya kaaranam norpaar
Silar palar nolaadhavar.
kurals.meaning: The reason so many in the world are destitute is that those who practise penance are few, and those who do not are many.
kurals.elementary: In a class, only a few kids practise every day, and most don’t. That is why only a few become really good. Valluvar says the same about the whole world: most people are ‘poor’ inside because only a few do the hard work of tapas.
kurals.university: The closing couplet uses a neat chiastic arithmetic — இலர் பலர் (the have-nots are many) because நோற்பார் சிலர், பலர் நோலாதவர் (the practisers are few, the non-practisers many). இலர் is ambiguous: Solomon Pappaiah reads material poverty, Varadarasan and Kalaignar read lack of strength, and Puliyur Kesikan reads lack of true knowledge. The choice matters: a literal economic reading makes tapas a cause of prosperity, while the spiritual reading makes it the cause of inner wealth. Either way the verse ends the chapter with a sober sociology of virtue — excellence is rare because discipline is rare — and turns the whole chapter into an exhortation to join the few.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Out of many thousands among men, one may endeavor for perfection, and of those who have achieved perfection, hardly one knows Me in truth.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna observes how rare the serious spiritual aspirant is.
hinduism.tie_back: The same ‘few strive, many don’t’ observation that grounds the Kural.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Rarity matches; the Kural adds the causal link to widespread lack.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat: Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts the many on the easy road with the few on the hard road to life.
christianity.tie_back: Same arithmetic of many and few, with the hard path as the source of true wealth.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the forerunners, the forerunners - … A [large] company of the former peoples And a few of the later peoples.”
islam.explanation: The foremost in devotion, brought nearest to God, are few among later generations.
islam.tie_back: The spiritually foremost are few, as the Kural’s practisers are few.
islam._accuracy_note: Rarity of the elite; no explicit causal claim about others’ lack.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai remarks that he has seen the ‘people of ascent’ — those of the highest spiritual rank — and they are few.
judaism.explanation: The Talmud acknowledges that those who reach the highest spiritual level are a small minority.
judaism.tie_back: Echoes the Kural’s ‘the practisers are few’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Few among men are those who cross to the farther shore. The rest, the bulk of men, only run up and down the hither bank.”
buddhism.explanation: Only a few achieve liberation; the majority stay in the round of existence.
buddhism.tie_back: Near-identical picture of the few who strive and the many who do not.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close; the Kural adds the causal ‘therefore many are destitute’.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sparta’s agoge subjected boys to hunger, cold, one cloak a year and harsh discipline; the few full citizens so trained dominated a far larger population of helots.
greek_mythology.explanation: Rigorous austerity produced a small elite of exceptional capability.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Illustrates the Kural’s claim that the disciplined few hold what the undisciplined many lack; but the Spartan aim was military, not spiritual.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Historical/civic rather than mythological or spiritual; next-best.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For as they say in the mysteries, ‘the thyrsus-bearers are many, but the mystics few’; and these mystics are, I believe, those who have been true philosophers.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates distinguishes the many who carry the outward emblems from the few who are genuinely initiated through philosophical purification.
philosophy.tie_back: The many/few contrast between those who merely participate and those who truly undergo the discipline.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close on the rarity of genuine practitioners.
